---
title: "Generators: Rules Behind the Record"
---

A record tells us what appeared. A generator tells us how another value could appear.

The distinction becomes visible when we ask for the next observation. A list can repeat a value already present in it. A generator must supply a rule for producing that value again.

## 🔰 A generator needs more than a list of possibilities {#sec-sample-generators-a-generator-needs-more-than-a-list-of-possibilities}

Consider a box that emits either zero or one. Knowing its alphabet $\{0,1\}$ leaves many possible rules:

- Alternate between zero and one.
- Toss a fair coin independently for each output.
- Toss once and repeat that result forever.
- Emit one whenever a temperature exceeds a threshold.

All produce binary signals. Their behavior across addresses differs.

A useful generator description specifies four things:

- **Values:** what it can emit.
- **State:** what it remembers between outputs.
- **Production rule:** how the next value is chosen from the current conditions.
- **Update rule:** what changes after that output.

Inputs from the environment may also affect production and update.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-sample-generator-state
%%| fig-cap: "A generator produces an output and updates its state. External inputs or a random source enter only when the model requires them."
flowchart TD
    S["Current state"] --> R["Production rule"]
    I["Inputs or random source"] --> R
    R --> V["Emitted value"]
    S --> U["State update"]
    I --> U
    V --> U
    U --> S
```

The feedback arrow gives memory a place in the architecture.

## 🏵 A distribution is one view of a generator {#sec-sample-generators-a-distribution-is-one-view-of-a-generator}

Suppose two machines both show zero or one with equal probability at any fixed address.

The first tosses independently at every step. The second tosses once and repeats forever.

For either machine, before a run begins,

$$
\mathbb P(X_t=0)=\mathbb P(X_t=1)=\frac12.
$$

But after observing the first output, their next outputs differ:

- For independent tosses, a first zero leaves the next toss equally balanced.
- For the repeating machine, a first zero determines every later output.

A distribution at one address cannot, by itself, describe these relationships between addresses.

This is why the presentation's generating structure $\mathsf F$ deserves to be larger than its potential profile $P[f]$.

## ⚙️ A deterministic rule can still be observed imperfectly {#sec-sample-generators-a-deterministic-rule-can-still-be-observed-imperfectly}

The alternating generator has a simple rule. If we do not know its starting phase, its next output may be uncertain to us.

A computer's pseudorandom generator also updates a state by a deterministic rule. Supplying the same initial state reproduces the sequence. Whether its output is suitable for a particular experiment requires more than checking whether a short record looks irregular.

We should distinguish the mechanism, what we know about it, and the statistical model used for its outputs. A complicated physical explanation need not be reconstructed before a useful probability model can be tested.

## 💡 Generation and inference face opposite ways {#sec-sample-generators-generation-and-inference-face-opposite-ways}

With a specified generator, we ask what records it could produce.

With a record in hand, we ask which generators remain consistent with it. Several may survive. Four alternating outputs could come from an alternating mechanism or from independent coin tosses.

The record constrains an explanation. A short record rarely determines it uniquely.

[Dice and Decks](dice-and-decks.qmd) gives us a generator whose state is easy to see and count.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try the idea {#sec-sample-generators-try-the-idea}

A machine emits $1,1,1,1$. Give two different rules compatible with this record. What additional observation would help distinguish them?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Work it through {#sec-sample-generators-work-it-through}

It might repeat its first coin toss forever, or toss independently and happen to produce four ones. A later zero would rule out the first description if the machine has not been reset. More ones would leave both possible, with different probabilities under the two models.
:::
